pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 9–11 — identify ways humans harm the ocean (plastic pollution, overfishing, oil spills, acidification from CO2) and understand that MOST ocean pollution comes from land-based activities, not just ships.
• Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2): Y6 'recognise the impact of… human activity on environments' and Y4 changing-environments strand; links to citizenship/geography.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-ESS3-1 (human activities affect Earth's resources/environment) and MS-ESS3-3/MS-LS2-4 (human impact and ecosystem disruption) — human effects on the ocean system.
• Operational details: two ideas — (1) NAME the main harms and how each hurts animals (plastic entangles/is eaten; overfishing removes species and collapses webs; oil coats/poisons; CO2 acidifies water); (2) the counter-intuitive KEY FACT that ~80% of marine pollution originates on LAND (runoff, litter, sewage, farm chemicals via rivers), not mainly from ships. Emphasise the invisible pathway from inland activity → rivers/runoff → sea. Build on ecosystem/food-web systems thinking so harms are traced as cascades.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~9): names ≥3 harms; Tier B (~10): explains one harm's effect on a marine animal and states most pollution comes from land; Tier C (~11): traces a land activity through runoff to a cascading effect in the ocean food web.
bestPractices: Correct the 'pollution comes from ships/at the sea' image head-on with the ~80%-from-land fact and the runoff pathway (inland → river → sea).
Make each harm concrete via its effect on a specific animal (turtle eating a plastic bag it mistakes for a jellyfish; seabird stomach full of plastic; otter coated in oil).
Trace harms as system cascades (overfishing one species → web disruption) using the ecosystem/food-web understanding already built.
Distinguish point-source (a single spill — dramatic but rarer) from nonpoint-source runoff (diffuse, cumulative, the bigger problem) so students grasp why land runoff dominates.
Keep it evidence-based and avoid guilt/doom framing; pair with the protecting-the-ocean topic so problems have solutions.
keyRepresentations: A land-to-sea pathway map: inland runoff/rivers carrying pollutants to the ocean
Harm–animal cards (plastic→turtle, oil→otter, overfishing→collapsed web, CO2→acidified water)
A food-web overlay showing a harm cascading through trophic levels
commonMisconceptions: 'Most ocean pollution comes from ships/dumping at sea' — the core misconception; ~80% is land-based via runoff.
'Pollution only affects the spot where it enters' — not seeing it spread and cascade through the web (e.g. via currents, bioaccumulation).
'Overfishing just means fewer of one fish' — missing the knock-on collapse of the wider ecosystem.
'Plastic goes away / breaks down quickly' — not knowing it persists and fragments into microplastics eaten by animals.
'If I live far from the sea, my actions don't affect the ocean' — ignoring the inland-runoff pathway.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: identify the main ways humans harm the ocean (plastic pollution, overfishing, oil spills, and acidification from CO2), and grasp the counter-intuitive key fact that roughly 80% of marine pollution originates on land — carried by runoff, litter, sewage and farm chemicals down rivers and drains to the sea — not mainly from ships. Learners name each harm and how it affects a specific marine animal, trace the invisible inland→river→sea pathway, and follow a harm as it cascades through the food web. Builds on prior ecosystem/food-web systems thinking.

activities.title: Live a day on land, then watch it reach the sea
feedback: When runoff carries a pollutant to sea, highlight that none of this happened at the sea itself — it began inland.
When the tally reaches roughly 80/20, note that about four-fifths of marine pollution comes from land, not ships (an approximate global estimate).
When overfishing is triggered, show the knock-on effect on other species, not just fewer of one fish.
If the learner expects ships to dominate, point to the growing land share and the river/drain pathway they just watched.
activities.rationale: The load-bearing idea is a source→pathway→consequence system; letting the child trigger inland actions and watch pollutants ride rivers to the sea and ripple through marine life is intended to make the invisible land–sea link that the '80% from land' fact names concrete. A live source tally (land vs ship) and a food-web overlay are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required mechanics.
sourceClaims: About 80% of pollution to the marine environment comes from the land (NOAA; the global figure is attributed by NOAA to a UN estimate), largely via nonpoint-source runoff rather than from ships.

The largest source of ocean pollution is nonpoint-source pollution carried by runoff from many diffuse inland sources (farms, vehicles, septic systems), contrasted with rarer point-source events like oil/chemical spills.

Marine debris (including plastic) comes overwhelmingly from people, with the majority originating on land and entering the ocean via littering, poor waste management and stormwater; plastic persists and is ingested by marine animals.
learnerActions: Look at a scene split between an inland town-and-farm on top and the ocean below.
Perform ordinary land actions: spread fertiliser on a field, drop a bottle by the kerb, flush the drains.
Trigger the rain and watch each pollutant wash into a stream, down a river, and out to sea.
Observe the consequences: the fertiliser feeds an algal bloom, and the bottle drifts out to sea and slowly breaks into fragments that a seabird or fish swallows, mistaking them for food.
Overfish a fish stock and watch the loss ripple visibly through a food-web overlay to other species.
Read a running source tally that shows land vs ship contributions, with land arriving at roughly four-fifths of the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Most ocean POLLUTION (about four-fifths) starts on LAND, often far from any ship, and travels via drains, runoff and rivers to the sea. Ocean harms, including pollution and overfishing (which happens at sea from fishing boats), can then cascade through the marine food web rather than staying at one spot.

activities.title: Harm–animal cards: naming harms through their victims
feedback: If only visible litter and spills are named, prompt that an invisible gas (CO2) dissolving into seawater also counts as pollution because it makes water more acidic and attacks shells and coral.
If the learner thinks plastic breaks down and disappears, note that it persists and fragments into microplastics that animals eat.
Confirm correct harm→animal matches with the specific mechanism (e.g. the turtle mistook the bag for a jellyfish).
activities.rationale: Making each harm concrete via a specific animal supports the evidence goal of naming at least three harms and describing how plastic or overfishing harms marine animals, and surfaces the misconceptions that plastic vanishes and that gases cannot be pollutants. A matching/sort can check classification but does not by itself elicit the learner's own explanation, so a state-it-yourself step is included.
sourceClaims: Marine debris (including plastic) comes overwhelmingly from people, with the majority originating on land and entering the ocean via littering, poor waste management and stormwater; plastic persists and is ingested by marine animals.
learnerActions: Match each harm to a specific animal and effect: plastic bag → turtle that eats it mistaking it for a jellyfish; plastic fragments → seabird with a stomach full of plastic; oil spill → otter with coated fur; overfishing → fewer fish left for seals and seabirds that eat them, disrupting the food web; CO2 → more acidic water that makes it harder for shellfish and coral to build and keep their shells and skeletons.
Name at least three distinct ways humans harm the ocean.
For one harm, state out loud or in writing exactly how it hurts a named animal.
activities.intendedInsight: Each ocean harm has a concrete, nameable effect on real animals; plastic persists and fragments into microplastics, and CO2 is an invisible gas that still pollutes the water.

activities.title: One bottle, many victims: tracing a cascade
feedback: If the learner says banning ships would clean the ocean, point out that around 80% starts on land via litter, runoff, sewage and chemicals, so most of the problem would remain.
If the learner says plastic only harms the one turtle that swallows it, follow microplastics or a toxin up the web to show one input reaching many victims.
Distinguish a single dramatic oil spill (point source, rarer) from diffuse everyday runoff (nonpoint source, the larger cumulative problem).
activities.rationale: This targets the discriminating idea that a child anchored on the 'ships and oil spills' image names only sea-based sources, while a child with the concept names a land pathway and a spreading mechanism. Contrasting point-source and nonpoint-source helps explain why land runoff dominates.
sourceClaims: The largest source of ocean pollution is nonpoint-source pollution carried by runoff from many diffuse inland sources (farms, vehicles, septic systems), contrasted with rarer point-source events like oil/chemical spills.
About 80% of pollution to the marine environment comes from the land (NOAA; the global figure is attributed by NOAA to a UN estimate), largely via nonpoint-source runoff rather than from ships.
learnerActions: Trace a plastic bottle dropped on a city street hundreds of miles from the coast to the sea, naming the route (drain → river → sea).
Follow a toxin or microplastic from plankton up through fish to predators, noting that one input can reach many animals that never touched the plastic directly.
Explain whether banning all ships would mostly stop ocean pollution, and why or why not.
Explain how carbon dioxide, a gas in the air, can count as ocean pollution.
activities.intendedInsight: Pollution does not stay where it enters: it spreads through currents and bioaccumulation up the food web, and because the bulk comes from land, stopping ship leaks alone would leave most of the problem untouched.

activities.title: Talking it through with a marine biologist or a sea turtle
feedback: Probe the learner's reasoning rather than simply confirming: ask them to say how the bottle actually travels or how the collapse spreads.
Pair the problem with solutions so the framing is empowering rather than guilt- or doom-laden.
Redirect to the land-to-sea mechanism if the dialogue drifts to ships as the main cause.
activities.rationale: Open dialogue may engage empathy and reasoning about responsibility and agency, complementing the modelled mechanism. Offered as a complement; the source row did not establish that dialogue teaches the empirical cascade better than a worked model.
learnerActions: Ask a marine-biologist character 'how does MY town's rubbish reach the sea?' and respond to their follow-up questions about the runoff pathway.
Discuss why overfishing hurts more than just one fish, explaining the web disruption in your own words.
Hear a turtle character recount mistaking a plastic bag for a jellyfish, and discuss what could be done differently.
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean harm has a values and agency dimension — who is responsible, whether distant inland behaviour matters, and what we can do — alongside the factual mechanism.

activities.title: Check: pollution sources, main cause, and a traced cascade
feedback: For the source item, reinforce that about four-fifths is land-based via runoff, litter, sewage and chemicals.
For the scenario, confirm the full chain (land activity → river/drain → sea → effect on an animal → spread through the web).
Recognition items check whether the idea is held; they do not by themselves show the learner can independently construct and explain the pathway, so pair with the explain/trace tasks above.
activities.rationale: Questions naming harms, a 'where does most pollution come from?' item, and a scenario tracing land activity to a marine effect map onto all three evidence goals. Recognition alone does not elicit production, so an open traced-chain task is included.
learnerActions: Name three ways humans harm the ocean.
Answer where most ocean pollution comes from — land or ships — and give the approximate share.
Work a scenario that traces a specific land activity through runoff to a cascading effect in the ocean food web.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can demonstrate naming harms, identifying the land-based majority source, and tracing a land activity to a cascading marine effect.

constraints: Correct the 'pollution comes from ships / at the sea' image directly using the ~80%-from-land fact and the inland→river→sea runoff pathway.
Keep framing evidence-based and avoid guilt or doom; pair problems with solutions (e.g. a protecting-the-ocean follow-up).

Distinguish point sources (a single identifiable source such as an oil spill or a sewage or factory pipe; a big spill is dramatic but rarer) from nonpoint-source runoff (diffuse and cumulative, often the larger problem). Note that land-based pollution includes both kinds.

A static pathway map or card set can present sources and effects clearly and cheaply; it is a valid exposition tool but does not itself let the child trigger a source and watch the cascade unfold, so pair it with an interactive or traced task for the systems insight. This is a scoped affordance, not a claim that only an interactive can teach the concept.

Recognition/multiple-choice items assess whether the concept is held but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the pathway explanation; include tasks where learners state or write the chain themselves.
The ~80% figure is an approximate global estimate (NOAA attributes it to a UN estimate); present it as 'about four-fifths', not an exact measured constant.
Build on prior ecosystem and food-web understanding so harms can be traced as cascades.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified here. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles/facts rather than proving any activity was tested.
The source row rated a 3D artefact as adding 'cost without deepening' the reasoning; this has been reframed as a narrowly scoped preference rather than a categorical claim that 3D adds nothing.
The original marked conversation and static image as not able to let the child trigger/watch the cascade; preserved as scoped affordance limits, not as 'only an interactive can teach this'.

The ~80% land-based figure is attributed by NOAA to a UN estimate; keep it as approximate. No arithmetic or force/motion content exists in this row to correct; the science (land-based majority, CO2 acidification, microplastic persistence, overfishing cascade) is consistent with the cited sources.

probeDeeper: A plastic bottle dropped on a city street hundreds of miles from the coast ends up in the sea. How does it get there?
If we banned all ships tomorrow, would ocean pollution mostly stop? Why or why not?
How can carbon dioxide — a gas in the air — count as ocean pollution?
One turtle swallows a plastic bag. Name one way that harm could reach animals that never touched any plastic.
assess.correctAnswer: No — most ocean pollution comes from LAND, not from ships. Around 80% of it starts on land: plastic litter, farm and sewage run-off, and chemicals wash down rivers and drains and out to sea, plus carbon dioxide from burning fuels dissolves into the water and makes it more acidic. Dramatic oil spills are real but are a small share of the total. So stopping ship leaks alone would leave most of the problem untouched, because the bulk pours off the land.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Ocean pollution mostly comes from ships and oil spills at sea' — the memorable disaster image stands in for the main cause.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the ~80%-from-land figure and trace a plastic bottle from a street drain down a river to the sea; ships are the exception, not the rule.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — ships and oil spills are the main source, so stopping leaks would make the ocean basically clean.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only ships, tankers and oil spills; leaves out rivers, drains, litter and run-off from land.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Pollution only hurts the animal that eats/meets it' — no sense of it spreading through the food web.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Follow microplastics or a toxin from plankton up through fish to predators; one input, many victims.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says plastic only harms the one turtle that swallows it; doesn't mention it moving up the web or breaking into microplastics.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Acidification is just rubbish/chemicals in the water' — doesn't see invisible CO2 gas as a pollutant.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain CO2 from burning fuels dissolving to form acid that lowers pH and attacks shells and coral — pollution you can't see.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists only visible litter and spills; surprised that a gas dissolving in seawater counts as harm.

responseLevels.gap: Names only ships/oil spills; believes the ocean would be clean if sea-based leaks stopped.
responseLevels.full: States most pollution is land-based (~80%), traces a land-to-sea pathway, and explains a specific harm mechanism (plastic through the food web, or CO2 → acidification) — transferring to judge whether a given action would fix much.
responseLevels.partial: Names several harms (plastic, overfishing, spills, acidification) but still frames pollution as sea-based, or can't say most of it comes from land.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says 'the ocean gets polluted mostly by ships and oil spills out at sea — so if we stopped ships leaking, the ocean would be basically clean'. Do you agree that ships are the main source? Where does most ocean pollution actually come from, and how does it get there?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child anchored on the vivid 'ships and oil spills' image names only sea-based sources and thinks the problem would be solved by fixing ships; a child with the concept says most pollution is land-based and can name a land pathway (rivers/drains/run-off) or the CO2-acidification route. The 'would the ocean be clean?' clause forces them to reveal whether they know where the bulk comes from.
